en: Preface to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*: Regarding the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*,
it is the virtuous foundation for accumulating pure karma and that which sweeps away the dust of worldly entanglements.
A moistening dew;
a ladder spanning the celestial realm, a vessel for crossing the sea of suffering.
It encompasses cause and effect, and embraces all blessings and benefits.
The principles are abundant while the words are concise; the style is vigorous while the meaning is elegant.
By giving rise to a single thought of pure faith, one ultimately parts from the four currents;
by initiating a single act of wholesome conduct, one finally ascends to the ten stages.
Thus the King of Physicians founded his enterprise,
and the General of the Dharma thereby attained universal penetration;
may it be that those of future generations may together observe this current and that its influence extends through distant eras.
Regarding the *Buddhabhāṣita-jentāka-saṃgha-snāpana-sūtra*:
it is indeed that which uses a torch to dispel the darkness within the cycle of birth and death,
standing alone and preeminent beyond the slumber of ignorance.
Having clarified all phenomena,
he awakened to the four modes of birth;
his enlightenment and practice were thus perfected.
Therefore, he is called a Buddha.
He unfurls the four types of eloquence from the tip of his tongue and flows forth the eight melodic tones for all to hear, [bestowing] the supreme merit of the seven stages.
It cultivates the fertile field of the Four Paths.
Disseminated from my own mouth, it penetrates the minds of others;
therefore, it is called [the teaching that] harmonizes the spirit as its goal.
The chamber uses the shape of the *kṣura* (razor) as its principle;
externally cleansing the eight objects of sensory dust is called "bathing," while internal cultivation is termed the "Sūtra of the Saṃgha."
Although there are five meanings, they are briefly subsumed under two, with two categories being cited:
first, the "gushing spring";
second, the "plumb line."
[The water] flows forth without exhaustion.
This principle can be likened to a constant line or a carpenter’s square used to establish what is correct.
Because this teaching clarifies its method, it is called the *Buddhabhāṣita-jentāka-saṃgha-snāna-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: Ānanda said... Thus at one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Magadha, on Mount Gayāśīrṣa. Commentary:
These three [sections] constitute the two introductory sequences; they mark the beginning and end of the textual flow.
The separate analysis of the preface follows.
This constitutes the "Testimony of Faith" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra, *Nidāna-parivarta*). [The Buddha’s] brothers... [text fragment].
The causal conditions established in previous lives mark the beginning of the arousal of the vow;
they intersect with the categories of sentient beings.
The blue lotus brings delight to the spirits of those who behold it;
furthermore, it causes the father king [to attain] such-and-such [merit].
Ānanda, that which I have heard from the Buddha is as follows:
To testify that one has heard it directly from the source, one says, "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*).
Regarding the transmission and reception [of the Dharma], there are two definitive meanings. First...
Regarding the two minds:
the determination of the mind constitutes the essence of faith.
[The text here is fragmentary: ...determination... ...the initial school holds that wisdom is the ultimate mystery; thus it is described at the outset as "Thus."
The expression "the auspicious time of transformation" (*huàchén*) refers to the occasion when the Dharma King inaugurates his mandate;
it is the moment when the great assembly rejoices. This [phrase] is also explained in the same manner as above.
Regarding the Mountain of Śiśumāragiri in the kingdom of Magadha:
it is the realm where [the Buddha] manifested his transformations;
the mountain is the place of his reliance and dwelling.
Those who dwell in the country do so for the sake of transforming the laity;
those who dwell in the mountains do so for the sake of [transforming] the assembly of monastics.
Magadha; this is translated as "the Land of the Virtuous Victor.
It is so named because of Mount Saṅkassa.
This is called Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak).
Within the city of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder whose son was named Jīvaka; he served as a great king of physicians.
The Master said: "The introductory section that follows consists of three parts."
First, the enumeration of the name of Jeta Grove;
second, the narration of the events concerning Jeta Grove.
There are five parts to this enumeration of the name.
First, the excellence of his field of knowledge;
second, the sublimity of his status;
third, the nobility of his lineage.
The four fingers [of the earth]... Jeta Grove in Rājagṛha is preeminent in its location;
there was a great elder of noble rank;
the name "Jeta" signifies that it is superior to the eight kingdoms; the King of Men established his residence here.
The Dharma King attained enlightenment therein;
the Physician King was born within that very place,
and for this reason it is preeminent.
There was a great elder of eminent rank and noble status named Jīvaka;
his fame spread throughout the eight kingdoms,
and his Way surpassed that of a hundred kings.
His benevolence extends even to the youngest children,
and his virtue stands preeminent among his peers;
since he has already been designated by the title "Elder" (Zhǎngzhě), [it is fitting that he be honored further].
The reason his rank is uniquely honored is that the lineage of Nāyī’s son is noble.
As for Nāyī, she was born from a *nāga*.
This woman’s physical constitution was extraordinary;
her descent of the spirit was likewise sagely,
as she received her vital breath from a fresh flower and was born from a wondrous cleft.
In reality, her manifested form was of such peerless beauty and such transcendent elegance that her exquisite countenance surpassed all others in the world.
For this reason,
she is called the daughter of the *nāga*;
since Jīvaka was of the lineage of the daughter of the *nāga*, he is known as such.
This is why it is so precious.
"Qiyu" (祇域) refers to the name.
"Qi" (祇) is the Sanskrit pronunciation.
This person is called "The Life-Giver.
He thoroughly understands the origins of the four types of illness and possesses a subtle mastery of the essentials of the eight medical arts.
If one applies acupuncture or administers medicine with such certainty, recovery is assured;
it is because he possesses this capacity that he is called "Able to Revive.
This explains why he is titled the Great King of Physicians, who skillfully cures all manner of illnesses.
One who prescribes medicine and administers treatment according to the needs of the illness is called a King of Physicians;
one whose treatments never fail to cure is termed a Skillful Healer;
and because of being a skillful healer, one is said to be "Able to Revive."

The Sūtra says: "He was fond of learning from a young age and became even more devoted as he grew up; his talents and skills were exceptionally proficient, and his wisdom reached mastery of the Five Classics, astronomy, and geography. Tong said:
"Next, to clarify the description of his virtues, there are three intended meanings."
First, the merit of cultivation;
second, the record of administrative achievements;
third, the concluding summary.
This is the achievement of the Three Beauties (mei-xue).
"Talent" (cai) refers to the Three Talents (san-cai):
Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.
The "arts" refer to the six arts:
ritual, music, archery, charioteering, writing, and mathematics.
The "five classics" are the five treatises on knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
The internal treatises refer to the Abhidharma-piṭaka; the treatises on logic, grammar, arts and crafts, and medicine.
Astronomy refers to the celestial bodies and lunar mansions;
geography refers to mountains and rivers.
Thus, because he revered the Way while young, it is said that "in his youth he loved learning.
Because he became increasingly earnest as he grew older, it is said that "his talents and arts were exceptionally proficient.
His wisdom was thorough and his mastery complete; thus, his prior love of learning was fulfilled.
The mastery of astronomy and geography is most excellent;

it is a profound penetration. The Scripture says: "In all that he governs, there is nothing that is not healed; the dead are restored to life, and funeral carriages are sent back. Tong said: [This is so].
This is the achievement of its clarification.
The first two lines offer a general praise;
the latter two lines provide a specific manifestation.
In the past, the efficacy [of medicine] was inconsistent;
those who met with untimely death had already ascended the path to the underworld,
yet upon encountering Jīvaka, they were restored.
The divine spirit was reawakened,
whereby the soul and breath were stilled and then restored to life;
the carriage was restrained, and the driver turned the chariot back.
It transforms misfortune into fortune and turns death toward life;
among efficacious spiritual responses, none is greater than this.
As the Sūtra says: "Its virtues are so numerous they cannot be fully recounted; the eight kingdoms revere it, and all who see it rejoice. Tong said:
This is the summary. Jīvaka,
your Way transcends the calculations of the mind.
His virtues are manifold and detailed; thus,
those who hear of them revere his character,
and those who behold him find their spirits gladdened.
The Sūtra says: "Thereupon, Jīvaka suddenly conceived a thought in the night: 'When morning comes, I shall go to the Buddha's dwelling and ask about my doubts.
The Commentary states: "The following narrative of the events naturally contains seven meanings."
First, the mind of resolve;
second, the initiation of effort;
third, the attainment of the goal.
Fourth, seeing the Buddha;
fifth, the entire Sangha;
sixth, hearing the Dharma.
Seventh is the activity of performing deeds;
this clarifies the generation of the mind.
Zhiyi, on an auspicious day when the night was tranquil and solemn, stirred his spiritual mind.
Having realized the primary cause for entering the Way,
he subsequently formed the intention to provide ablutions for the monks.
Thus, although the thought resided within himself, it was directed toward others.
The Dharma is not something one can obtain through mere willpower.
This is why he sat in expectation until the dawn, when he approached the Buddha to request a definitive resolution.
The Sūtra says: "At dawn, he commanded his household and all his kinsmen to prepare themselves and proceed solemnly to the place where the Buddha was. Tong said:
As the funeral procession set forth,
the morning star suddenly obscured its brilliance,
and the rising sun gradually spread its light.
Having already observed the omens of the painted finger,
one ought to earnestly observe the admonitions for leading the host;
thus, it was first signaled at the break of dawn.
Thereafter, he immediately issued an edict to his family.
However, seeking the Way at this time was not merely for his own benefit;
he wished to cause his grace to extend to his nine branches of kin.
The Way permeates the six types of kin;
men and women share in its glory, and those of high and low station alike are moistened by it. This is why, when facing the crossroads, he brings order to the multitude.
His followers were as numerous as clouds;
great and small traveled together,
all following the path of the Buddha.
The Sutra says: "He arrived at the gate of the vihāra. Tong said:
"This indicates a place of profound understanding.
Since Jīvaka’s depth of inquiry regarding the Way was already deep,"
Therefore, the celestial carriage was able to journey to the divine pavilion;
thus it is said that he arrived at the gate of the vihāra.
As the Sūtra says: "He beheld the Buddha resplendent, his light illuminating heaven and earth. Tong said:
This clarifies the vision of the Buddha.
When the Tathāgata was about to kindle the torch of wisdom, he first emitted light from his countenance;
thus, the sun and moon spread their brilliance, and the heavens and rivers were illuminated through and through.
The Sūtra says: "The assembly of the fourfold congregation numbered in the tens of millions. The Commentary states:
This clarifies the universal community of monks (*saṃgha*).
Although the Tathāgata’s virtue is uniquely eminent, it is also due to the veneration of the multitude.
Thus, the assembly of the fourfold followers numbered in the tens of millions, like a sandalwood grove surrounded by sandalwood trees.
The Sūtra says: "The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they listened with single-minded tranquility. The Commentary says:
This clarifies the hearing of the Dharma.
The Sangha already looks up to the Buddha’s virtues;
the Buddha, in turn, fans them with the profound wind [of the teachings].
Since the way of teacher and disciple has been made manifest, the protocol for listening [to the Dharma] is likewise established.
The Sūtra says: "The retinue of Jīvaka alighted from their carriage, proceeded directly forward, prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and each sat to one side. The Commentary says:
This clarifies his karmic activity.
Jīvaka came because he wished to inquire about the Way;
for this reason, [the Buddha] alighted from his carriage.
Since harmony and tranquility are our ultimate refuge,
I shall proceed directly to set forth my initial report; yet, out of reverent concern for the fourfold assembly,
I have remained at a respectful distance from each of you.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha consoled him, saying, "Welcome, King of Physicians! Should you wish to ask anything, do not hesitate or find it difficult. The Commentary says:
The preceding section clarifying the introduction is now complete; the following section clarifies the body of the scripture.
Next, the benefits of sitting immediately [in meditation] are clarified.
The essence of the sūtra itself possesses five aspects.
The first is "drawing up."
Second, the request;
third, the praise and exposition;
fourth, the answering of questions.
Fifth is the severing of doubts;
this refers to the drawing forth [of beings].
The establishment of this teaching relies upon the Medicine King as its instrumental cause.
He greeted him with "Welcome" to comfort his mind and urged him to proceed with his questions without hesitation.
The Sūtra says: Jīvaka knelt down with palms joined and addressed the Buddha. Tong said:
The following clarifies that the formal invitation contains five intentions:
first, to express solemnity;
second, to lament one's own [failings]; and third, to request the performance [of the rite].
The fourth is making vows and the fifth is requesting grace; these now manifest solemnity.

However, when petitioning for a matter according to principle, one must further adjust one’s physical demeanor; it is for this reason that one kneels long before speaking to offer a formal announcement.

The Sūtra says: "Though they have attained transcendence, they remain aloof and wild among the worldly masses; though following the common stream, they have never cultivated merit. The Commentary says:
This expresses self-lamentation.
When the mind wanders among external objects, it is called "aloof" (shu).
To have one’s form fall among the mundane is to be a "wild" person.
Being wild, one follows the common currents of the world;
being negligent, one has never performed meritorious deeds.
The Sūtra says: "I now wish to invite the Buddha and the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas to enter the bathhouse for a thorough cleansing. The Commentary says:
"To 'invite' means to lead them forth.
Thus, the physical ailments of sentient beings may be roughly treated."
The remains of the Sage have never been requested for a ritual bath;
yet, as we now wish to establish the foundation of pure karma, we must rely upon a fertile field.
For this reason, we respectfully invite the Three Honored Ones to visit our humble abode.
The Sūtra says: "May sentient beings, throughout the long night, be pure, with defilements eliminated and no longer beset by manifold afflictions. The Commentary says:
This is the making of a vow.
The acts of "leading" and "vowing" are practiced in tandem.
It is like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird; by means of them,
one travels over land or flies through the air.
Neither one can be omitted;
therefore, in requesting [the practice], one must further make vows.
Vows and practices.
May this vow universally benefit all the common people,
forever dispelling the afflictions of defilement and burden,
and eternally securing the peace and well-being of lightness and ease.
The Sūtra says: "Only by the Buddha’s sacred will shall my aspirations not be neglected. The Commentary states:
This is a petition for grace.
May the Buddha’s sacred will illuminate my humble mind.
It is not that he neglects his aspirations, for he has personally descended into this chamber.
The Sūtra says: "The Buddha addressed the King of Physicians: 'Excellent, O One of Wondrous Intent! The Commentary states:
"The following clarifies the exposition."
There are four intentions:
first, the beautiful mind;
second, the description of karma.
Third, he manifested his merit;
fourth, he granted permission to proclaim it.
This is the noble intention of his mind.
Since Jīvaka both despised the mind of rustic seclusion and cherished the resolve to cultivate merit,
he was able to set his heart upon pure karma and come here to travel and inquire about the Way.
Because this is the truly wondrous intention, it is praised as "Excellent.
The Sūtra says: "He treats the illnesses of the multitudes, and all receive healing; those far and near rely on his blessings, and there are none who do not rejoice. The Commentary says:
This describes the consequences of past karma.
Since one already possesses a body, who can be free from affliction?
Since one continues to possess consciousness, who does not fear suffering?
Since Jīvaka was able to administer medicinal herbs so that they took effect immediately,
he could transform suffering into happiness;
and as soon as he applied needles and moxibustion, he could change a premature death into a long life.
Therefore, those who have already been treated immediately experience mutual joy and reliance;
even those not yet cured likewise form bonds of joyful resolve in anticipation.
As the Sūtra says: "Now we further invite the Buddha and the assembly of monks to bathe; may this merit extend to the ten directions. Tong said:
This describes newly performed deeds;
it requests the Sangha to describe their practices;
and it describes vows for the ten directions.
Nevertheless, since the practice must be directed toward specific matters, it has hitherto been limited to this region alone.
I wish to set up a banner that extends beyond, spreading throughout other lands;
thus it is said, "I pray that it may reach the ten directions."
The Sūtra says: "When various medicines treat illness and bathing removes impurities, the merit thereof is immeasurable. The Commentary says:
This demonstrates that merit;
for when the mind that treats disease is expansive, [the merit is likewise vast].
The vow to wash the monks was further expanded;
since one has planted infinite causes,
one shall therefore receive immeasurable retribution.
The Sūtra says: "Listen with a single mind to the Dharma; I shall first explain for you the merit of bathing the Saṃgha and making offerings to them.
The Commentary states: This permits his preaching.
Jīvaka came to bathe the monks.
Therefore, as for the retribution previously mentioned,
since the request was not made because of illness,
it is appropriate that the fruit of treating the illness be suspended.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Jīvaka that the method for bathing should employ seven substances to eliminate seven ailments and obtain seven rewards of merit. The Commentary states:
From here below, the answer to the question consists of three sections.
First, the heading;
second, the explanation;
third, the verse.
This constitutes the headings:
first, the heading for the substance of the seven objects;
second, the heading for the function of the seven objects.
Regarding the retribution for the three signs and seven items, the Sūtra says:

"What are the seven items? First, fire; second, pure water; third, soaked beans; fourth, clarified butter; fifth, thick ash; sixth, willow twigs; seventh, an undergarment. These constitute the method for bathing. Tong said:
This enumerates the seven substances.
When fire is kindled, it blazes with intense flames, extinguishing light smoke until no flame remains.
When pure water is clarified, it becomes like a mirror, removing all turbidity while retaining its clarity.
The soaked beans are both slippery and lustrous;
the su-fat is congealed yet its substance remains moist.
Pure lye is pungent and fierce, burning through the wood of the mountain mulberry.
The tooth-sticks are fine and supple, fashioned from the slender twigs of river willows;
as for the undergarments,
they are made of newly torn, even white silk.
The whiteness was like that of fine silk;
the tailoring was exquisite,
and the design was novel.
Although these are merely the inner garments among humans,
they are the superior robes among the gods; since these seven substances are so exquisite,
if these seven rewards were as beautiful as those, they would be truly magnificent.
The merits of this are described in the subsequent text.

The Sūtra says: "What are the seven things that cure illness? First, the stability of the four great elements; second, the removal of wind disorders; third, the removal of dampness and numbness; fourth, the removal of cold and chills; fifth, the removal of heat and fever; sixth, the removal of impurities and filth; seventh, lightness and ease of body and clarity of eyes. These are what remove the illnesses of the Saṃgha. Tong said:
This reveals the efficacy of the seven substances:
the function of the four great elements is to provide stability for the inner garments;
the function of the pure ash is to eliminate wind disorders.
The function of clarified butter is to remove dampness and rheumatism;
the function of kindling a fire is to dispel cold and ice;
the function of a willow branch is to eliminate heat and vapors.
The function of the *tila* beans is to remove impurities;
the function of the pure water is to make the body light and agile and the eyes clear and sharp.
Why is this? For when the body is covered by clothing, the four limbs are at peace, even though they may be ugly.
Ashes dispel wind-related ailments so that the six sense organs may become peaceful and pure;
medicinal ointments eliminate numbness according to the prescribed formulas;
and kindling fire wards off the cold while retaining warmth.
In bringing fragrance and removing stench, nothing is more excellent than the *yángzhī* (willow branch).

In cleansing the body and removing impurities, nothing surpasses the addition of *sēndòu* (soapberry). Furthermore, water possessing the eight virtues is uniquely endowed with all such manifold beauties.
Thoroughly washing both the internal and external, it brings elegant clarity to the breast and chest;
it brightens the eyes and refines the body, soaking away witheringness and removing turbidity.
When these seven merits are thus like mist, [the mind becomes clear].
The seven ailments likewise vanish like clouds;
therefore it is said, "This is for the purpose of removing the seven ailments of the Saṃgha.
The Sūtra says: "By making offerings in this manner, one obtains seven blessings. What are these seven blessings? The General Response says:
From here below, the retribution for the seven types of objects is clarified.
This section consists of three parts.
First, obtaining a corresponding fruit.
Second, one obtains the fruit of retribution;
third, one obtains the sovereign fruit.
This clarifies that because one obtains fruits similar [to their causes], the number is indicated to pose the question.

The Sūtra says: "First, when the four great elements are at peace and free from illness, one will give birth to those who are peaceful, brave, martial, and robust, whom the multitude admires and respects. The Commentary says:
This is like the fruit of kindling a fire.
When warm energy flows through the form, the entire body is peaceful and at ease;
when cold winds invade the bones, the whole body trembles with fear.
Because one kindles fire to bring forth warmth, one receives the retribution of a body that is secure and robust.
When one is both at ease and robust, the multitude will look up to them with reverence. As the Sūtra says: "Second, those born [with such qualities] have pure faces and upright features;

dust and water do not adhere to them, and they are respected by others. The Commentary states: When one is both at ease and robust, the multitude will look up to them with reverence. As the Sūtra says: "Second, those born [with such qualities] have pure faces and upright features; dust and water do not adhere to them, and they are respected by others. The Commentary states: The meaning is that when one’s body is healthy and free from illness, and one’s mind is tranquil and free from affliction, one naturally inspires awe and respect in others. This is because a person who is physically and mentally composed possesses an inner power that manifests outwardly. Furthermore, it indicates that such a person has cultivated their conduct and virtues over many lifetimes, resulting in a physical presence that is inherently dignified and serene. Thus, even without speaking, their very appearance commands the respect of all who behold them. This is the second mark of a person destined for greatness.
This is pure water resembling fruit.
Now, as for water:
first, it can purify others.
Second, because his nature is pure and clean;
as his face and features are upright and naturally pure,
dust and water do not adhere to him.
His facial features were as pristine as the full moon, untouched by dust or water;
he resembled a red lotus. Having attained such a moon-like and lotus-like appearance, all who beheld him felt both love and reverence.
The Sūtra says: "Third, his body is always fragrant and his clothing is clean and pure; those who see him rejoice and all pay him respect.
The Commentary says: This is the fruit similar to the seed.
When the physical form is soiled and greasy, filth and impurity proliferate;
when its substance is fresh and bright, fragrance wafts forth.
The efficacy of the bean paste can subsequently illuminate the body and remove its grime.
The retribution one receives is such that one’s clothing is pure and the body is fragrant.
Being both pure and fragrant, those who behold one find their spirits sustained.

As the Sūtra says: "The four limbs are moist and lustrous; his majestic radiance and virtue are so great that all without exception revere and praise him. He walks alone without peer. The Commentary states:
This is the fruit that resembles medicinal ointment.
When the numbness and defilements pervade the four limbs, the skin becomes stiff and tough;
when the ointment flows through the hundred joints, the pores and tissues become harmonious and supple.
Since the application of medicinal ointments dispels numbness and harmonizes the body,
one receives a retribution of majestic radiance and supple skin.
Possessing both this radiance and suppleness, one walks alone without equal.
Since he walks alone without peer, who would not revere and honor him?

The Sūtra says: "Fifth, many people follow him; as he brushes away dust and grime, they naturally receive blessings; he constantly remembers his past lives. The Commentary states: The Sūtra says: "Fifth, many people follow him; as he brushes away dust and grime, they naturally receive blessings; he constantly remembers his past lives. The Commentary states: [as above].
This is the fruit that resembles pure ash.
For when dust and filth defile the body, the wind causes consciousness to become昏 (obscured);
because ash can remove this filth, it is so named.
Many people use it to brush away dust;
furthermore, it can also disperse the wind.
For this reason, one constantly perceives past lives.
The Sūtra says: "Sixth, his mouth and teeth are fragrant and fine, being square, white, and even; whatever teachings he proclaims are all received with solemnity. The Commentary says:
"This is a fruit similar to that of the *yānjī* (willow-branch)."
As for the willow branch, chewing it removes heat from the mouth;
thus it causes the fragrance of the teeth to manifest and becomes clear and bright,
while the luster of the teeth is brought to a state of whiteness.
Since fragrance is without stench and teeth are white, what one speaks is wondrous and is received by others. The Sūtra says:
"Seventh, in the place where one is born, garments appear spontaneously, adorned with radiant and precious jewels, such that those who see them are struck with awe. The Commentary says:
This inner garment is a result that corresponds to its cause.
Now, as for an inner garment:
internally, it conceals what is ugly.
Externally, they maintain a dignified appearance to conceal their ugliness;
by birth, they are naturally provided with clothing.
Because of his dignified appearance, he further adorned himself with precious jewels.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Jīvaka: "Abiding in this practice of bathing the assembly of monks, the bodhisattva gains these seven blessings. The commentary states:
The detailed exposition having been completed, this serves as a further summary. The Sūtra says:

"By virtue of these causes and conditions, one may become a minister or a sovereign; or a sun-god, a moon-god, or one of the four heavenly kings; or Śakra, the King of Devas, or a Cakravartin Golden Wheel-turning King; or be born in the Brahma Heaven to receive immeasurable blessings; or become a Bodhisattva who resolves the mind, cultivates the stages, perfects his merit, fulfills his vows, and ultimately attains Buddhahood. The General Commentary states:
This clarifies the attainment of karmic retribution.
Alternatively, one may become a minister,
belonging to the class of the Three Ducal Ministers and Nine High Officials.
Sometimes they become emperors and kings, such as the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors;
sometimes they become the sun, the moon, or the Four Heavenly Kings,
each presiding over one quarter of the world.
A Wheel-Turning Sage King exercises sovereign authority over the four quarters,
or is born in the Brahma Heaven as a reward for attaining meditative concentration.
Or they become bodhisattvas,
ascending toward the fruit of world-transcendence.
Thus, the initial resolve is the aspiration to dwell [in this state].
The stage of cultivating the ground (*bhūmi-karman*) is the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);
the arrival at merit is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*);
and the fulfillment of the vow is the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-mārga*).
Thus, one attains Buddhahood; this is the stage of liberation.
The Sūtra says: "The reason for this is that by making offerings to the Sangha—the immeasurable field of merit—one is not harmed by drought or flood. Tong said:
This clarifies that one attains the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
By making offerings to the Sangha—the field of merit—one sows the seeds;
that these are not harmed by drought or flood is the attainment of the retribution (*vipākaphala*).
Even the fire that melts gold and fuses stone cannot describe its parching power;
nor can the waters of the great rivers upon the mountains.
"How could it possibly sink into water or burn in fire?
Since it is neither subject to drought nor flood, what harm could there be? Tong said:
The prose is for the purpose of explaining the meaning;
the verses are for the purpose of retention.
There are twenty verses in total.
The three sections are extensively opened.
The first verse provides a general heading to command the audience to listen;
the subsequent eighteen verses proclaim the sacred teachings according to specific matters.
The final verse concludes with joy, harmonizing the field [of merit].
In the general heading, it says "shadows of merit" (*yingfu*):
merit follows its causes just as a shadow follows a form.
The Holy Xuanzhong’s commentary on the preceding verses on the fruits of retribution is divided into nine sections.
The first verse praises the common people;
the second consists of two verses praising the ministers.
The third pair of verses praises the human kings;
the fourth single verse praises the Four Heavenly Kings;
and the fifth single verse praises the sun and moon.
The sixth pair of verses praises Śakra;
the seventh pair of verses praises the Wheel-Turning King;
and the eighth pair of verses praises the Emanated Response.
The ninth pair of verses praises Brahmā.
The thirteenth verse praises the Bodhisattva Śakra;
as for the name "Śakra," it is called Indrāli.
Regarding the sixth, the Heaven of Transformation and Response (Nirmāṇarati):
because in the fifth heaven beings transform themselves and respond to themselves without external responses coming to them,
it is not called the Heaven of Transformation and Response.
Because the sixth heaven spontaneously manifests others as external responsive transformations,
it is called the Heaven of the Kings of Transformational Response (Nirmāṇarati).
As for "the excellent merit of the four paths":
The four paths of the śramaṇas constitute the fertile field.

The Sūtra says: After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he told Jeta that he observed how the various classes of devas and humans within the three realms differ in their status—high or low, long or short, and the amount of their merit—all of which result from the inequality of their mental applications in previous lives, and thus they receive retributions that are each distinct and not the same. Tong said:
Next, the clarification of the elimination of doubts is explained:
first, the practice for eliminating doubts;
second, the vow for eliminating doubts.
Regarding this practice for severing doubt, which is termed "principle" yet functions as cause and effect:
since they share the same single cause, they ought to attain a single fruit;
now, since the cause that can wash away [defilements] is indeed one.
How can the fruits obtained be so vastly different?

Is there then a distinction between humans and devas, or between ordinary beings and sages; a difference based on the degree of one's virtuous intent or the extent of one's practice? Do you judge length by the physical form and determine high or low by outward appearance?
To sever this doubt, the Buddha said:
"All [result] from the inequality of the mind applied in previous lives; it is entirely due to this. Why is that?
Although their practices are the same,
their aspirational minds differ; as for practice,
it is that which can be accomplished.
Aspiration can lead;
practice can cause existence or non-existence;
aspiration can cause superiority or inferiority.
If one’s aspirational mind prays for that which transcends the world,
one will immediately attain the fruit of transcendence;
if one’s aspirational mind seeks that which belongs to the world, [one will attain that].
One immediately obtains worldly retribution;
for this reason, what is received differs.
The Sūtra says: "Such reception of the Dharma and its meritorious rewards are all obtained solely by bathing the assembly of noble Saṃghas. The Commentary says:
This is the vow for severing doubt.
The doubt is as follows:
"If practice, though it is one,"
If [liberation] were determined by the differences in one's vows,
then one should simply make vows to attain the supreme fruit for oneself;
why is it necessary to engage in practice and undergo such strenuous toil?
Now, it is explained that the aspiration is difficult to fulfill because it must be drawn forth by the power of practice; for if there were no practice, what would the aspiration have to draw forth?
The practice that is thus drawn forth is precisely the purification of the Saṃgha.
He said: "Such meritorious rewards are all obtained solely from bathing the assembly of sages.

The Sūtra says: After the Buddha had finished preaching the Sūtra, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what name should this Sūtra be called, and by what means should it be used for exhortation? The Commentary says:
This clarifies the third section, the dissemination [of the teaching].
It contains two internal points:
first, it clarifies the methods for instruction provided by the attendant.
The subsequent section clarifies how Jīvaka fulfilled his lifelong commitment;
this constitutes the first chapter, which itself contains two inquiries.
Examining the text to seek its headings:
What is the title of this text?
The subsequent question concerns its meaning in terms of "hearing and upholding.
How is this meaning explained as an exhortation? The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Ānanda, "This sūtra is titled 'The Sūtra on Bathing the Assembly of Monks in a Warm Chamber. The commentary says:
This answers the first question.
Since this sutra takes the washing of the Sangha as its reality,
it is named according to this very reality.

The Sūtra says: "That which is recorded by all Buddhas was not created by me alone; when a practitioner attains liberation, it is not bestowed by a deity. One who seeks pure merit should naturally practice for oneself. The Commentary says: [This means that] the teachings transmitted by the Buddhas are not my own invention; rather, when a practitioner attains deliverance, it is not something granted by a supernatural spirit. Those who seek the merit of purity should personally and diligently carry out the practice.
This answers the subsequent question.
Because it is that which has been prophesied by all Buddhas, it can be used for exhortation;
because practitioners thereby attain deliverance, it can be used for instruction.
Because it can be used for encouragement,
those who practice together will surely enter together.
Because it can be used for such instruction.
One who performs an action receives its retribution oneself;
therefore, it is said that it is not the *ātman* (spirit/soul) that receives it.

The Sūtra says: "When the Buddha had finished speaking this, Jīvaka and his retinue heard the Sūtra with joy, attained the stage of *Srotāpanna*, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew. He then prepared and arranged the washing implements. The Commentary says:
This is precisely Jīvaka’s expression of his intent to offer service.
Since Jīvaka’s roots of the Path have long been established, he has heard the sutras and protected the fruits [of his practice].
Nevertheless, his request was not made in vain.
They requested to depart after having prepared themselves with solemnity.
The Sūtra says: "The assembly, both great and small, each having attained the tracks of the Path, all together prostrated themselves in worship and departed. Tong said:
"Since they had come together for the same purpose of requesting [instruction],..."
Thus, the fruit is not realized alone;
therefore, when Jīvaka beheld the footprints,
both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were moistened by his grace.
Now that the hearing of the Dharma has concluded and the attainment of the Way has been fully realized,
it is necessary to manifest solemnity.
Having presented his respects, he adjusted his robes and immediately changed his demeanor; thus it is said that "he performed a prostration and departed.
Compiled by Huìjìng as a commentary on the *Wēnshì jīng* (The Scripture of the Warm Bath).
